**Answer**

The primary male hormone is **testosterone**, and it is **derived from cholesterol**.  
During steroidogenesis, cholesterol is the single, obligatory precursor that is converted in Leydig cells of the testes (and to a lesser extent in the adrenal cortex) to pregnenolone, which is then processed through a series of enzymatic steps to produce testosterone.  

**Source**

## [Organ-Specific Toxicologic Pathology]

[2002, Handbook of Toxicologic Pathology (Second Edition)]Dianne M. Creasy, Paul M.D. Foster

### 5. Testosterone Synthesis

[Leydig cells] are the major site for the synthesis of the predominant male [steroid hormone], testosterone. Cholesterol is the obligatory intermediate in the synthesis of testosterone and is supplied to the [Leydig cell] either by receptor-mediated [endocytosis] of [lipoprotein] or by _de novo_ synthesis from acetate. The rate-limiting step in testosterone synthesis is the metabolism of cholesterol to [pregnenolone] by the [side chain cleavage enzyme] complex. This is a [cytochrome] P450-containing enzyme located in the mitochondria. The remainder of the process occurs outside the mitochondrion, principally on the smooth [endoplasmic reticulum]. From pregnenolone, two metabolic routes, termed Δ 4 and Δ 5 pathways, are thought to operate (Fig. 10), depending on the species. All of the intermediates have been isolated from testicular tissue. Following secretion from the Leydig cell, testosterone is metabolized further in the liver, androgen-dependent tissues and a variety of peripheral tissues (Figs. 10 and 11).

![Image 2]

[Sign in to download full-size image]

Figure 10. The synthesis and metabolism of testosterone in various compartments. Testosterone can be produced by two different pathways termed Δ4 and Δ5, the predominant pathway being species specific. Pregnenolone is produced from cholesterol by the side chain cleavage enzyme in the mitochondrion; the remainder of the synthesis takes place in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. Testosterone and androstenedione can be converted into estradiol and estrone, respectively, by the activity of aromatase. This can occur within the testis but occurs mainly in peripheral tissues. In the epididymal epithelium and the epithelium of the prostate and seminal vesicles, testosterone underoes 5α reduction to produce the main androgen for these tissues: dihydrotestosterone. Further metabolism to 3α or 3β diols also occurs. In the liver, metabolism to 17-ketosteroids allows for urinary excretion following conjugation with glucuronic or sulfuric acid.

Reproduced with permission from Creasy (1999).Copyright © 1999 

![Image 3]

[Sign in to download full-size image]

Figure 11. Major endocrine and paracrine pathways regulating male reproductive function. The main hormone testosterone (T) secreted by the Leydig cell (LC) in response to luteinizing hormone (LH) from the pituitary, which is under the control of the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secreted from the hypothalamus. The follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which acts on the Sertoli cell (SC), also has a permissive role in the maintenance of spermatogenesis and is positively regulated by activin (A) and negatively controlled by inhibin (I) secreted by the Sertoli cell. In response to testosterone, the Sertoli cell secretes a variety of proteins (androgen-regulated proteins), which modulate germ cell (GC) development. One of these proteins, androgen-binding protein, binds and acts as a transport protein for testosterone within the seminiferous tubule fluid (T-ABP). Androgen receptors on the blood vessels (BV) and peritubular myoid cells (MC) also enable testosterone to regulate blood flow and vascular permeability as well as tubular contractility. The regulation is a two-way process with factors being secreted by the target cells back to the Leydig cells. Testosterone enters the peripheral circulation and is also transported by the seminiferous tubule fluid to the secondary sex tissues where it is converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and to peripheral tissues such as adipose tissue where it is converted into estradiol (E). DHT and estradiol maintain secondary sexual characteristics and provide regulatory feedback to the hypothalamic–pituitary axis.

**Answer**

The primary male hormone is **testosterone**, and it is **derived from cholesterol**.  
During steroidogenesis, cholesterol is the single, obligatory precursor that is converted in Leydig cells of the testes (and to a lesser extent in the adrenal cortex) to pregnenolone, which is then processed through a series of enzymatic steps to produce testosterone.  

**Source**  
- ScienceDirect – “Testosterone synthesis” (overview): *“Leydig cells are the major site for the synthesis of the predominant male steroid hormone, testosterone. Cholesterol is the obligatory intermediate in the synthesis of testosterone…”*【commentary:7】
